title: Kilwa's merchants connected East Africa to Asia
body: From the 13th to the 16th century, the Swahili port of Kilwa Kisiwani in present-day Tanzania traded with Arabia, India and China. Gold from inland Africa passed through a port where imported ceramics arrived.
takeaway: A fragment of pottery can preserve the route of a trade that left little paperwork.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara
visual: a dhow near the stone waterfront of a medieval Swahili trading port

title: Bagan's monuments record centuries of Buddhist giving
body: Bagan in central Myanmar reached its height as the capital of a regional empire in the 11th to 13th centuries CE. Building and donating religious monuments was a way to earn merit, or spiritual benefit.
takeaway: An act of giving repeated over generations can change the shape of an entire city.
visual: temple spires rising from the mist across the Bagan plain

title: A printed book from China carries the date 11 May 868
body: The Diamond Sutra is a Buddhist text printed in China from carved wooden blocks. Its dated note at the end makes the scroll one of the earliest surviving examples of printing that can be placed on an exact day.
takeaway: The date fixes an example of book printing centuries before Gutenberg's press.
source: Jeremy Norman, History of Information, The Diamond Sutra
visual: a partly rolled ancient paper scroll seen from the back beside a carved woodblock

title: Benin's palace once lined its columns with brass reliefs
body: Around 1600, an account of the royal palace at Benin described wooden pillars covered with decorated brass plaques. Artists working for the court cast these reliefs from wax models.
takeaway: Plaques now displayed as separate objects once formed a larger architectural record of court life.
source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Art of Africa: A Resource for Educators
visual: a relief plaque of a court figure attached to a dark wooden pillar
